uses: Mullein is a traditional chest herb: its soft, slippery leaves and flowers were steeped in milk or water for coughs, and old country names such as bullock's lungwort recall farmers giving it to cattle with a cough. The EMA recognizes the flowers as a traditional remedy for a sore throat with a dry cough and cold. In folk practice the flowers were left in olive oil in the sun to make an oil rubbed on bruises and frostbitten skin, and Culpeper used the leaves in warm baths for stiff, cramped muscles. The dry down made tinder and lamp wicks, and the flowers gave a golden hair rinse and yellow dyes.
taste: Leaves mucilaginous and slightly bitter; flowers mild and mucilaginous
energetics: Culpeper called mullein somewhat dry, with a cleansing quality
caution_pregnancy: Safety during pregnancy and breastfeeding has not been established, and the EMA does not recommend mullein then. Not enough is known; avoid.
caution_medications: The EMA reports no known interactions with medicines.
caution_conditions: The fine, rough hairs on the leaves and flowers can irritate the throat and other tender membranes, so always strain mullein tea and oil through a coffee filter or fine cloth; a sieve isn't enough. See a doctor if a cough brings shortness of breath, fever or phlegm containing pus, or gets worse. The EMA does not recommend it for children under 12, or for anyone allergic to it. Grieve notes the seeds are slightly narcotic and were thrown into water by poachers to stun fish, and Ohio State's weed guide says the leaves and seeds may cause sleepiness if eaten in quantity; don't use the seeds.
caution_duration: If a sore throat or cough lasts more than a week, see a doctor or qualified practitioner.
caution_topical: Handling the furry leaves and stems can bring on a skin rash (contact dermatitis), and herbalists report itching when the leaves touch tender skin, so take care using them on bare skin. The flowers are hairy too, so filter infused oil well.
garden_harvest_timing: Second-year plants flower over the summer; each bloom opens in the dark before sunrise and shuts in the afternoon, so pick open flowers in the morning.
garden_water: Drought-tolerant; likes dry, sandy or rocky, well-drained soil and won't stand wet ground
notes: A biennial: a felted grey rosette the first year, then a single flower spike 5 feet or more tall that dies after setting seed. The seed needs light to sprout and can stay alive in the soil for decades, and it is listed as a noxious weed in some US states. Bees and other pollinators visit it. Grieve records that mullein was said to drive off evil spirits, that witches were believed to light their lamps with its wicks, and that some held it was the plant Ulysses carried against Circe. Culpeper places mullein under Saturn.
